methodology: The BareBoard Hot 100 ranks devices by estimated interest to the hardware-hacking community. Ordering reflects editorial judgment weighing: (1) repairability and design openness (modular, documented, open-hardware devices rank higher); (2) chip-level curiosity (novel, custom, or first-of-kind silicon); (3) documented teardown activity (iFixit or community teardowns); and (4) hackability (unlockable bootloaders, custom firmware scenes, modding communities). Version 2.0 expands the ranking from 100 to 150 devices; new entries (ranks 101-150) were appended below the original ranking and carry the same evidence standards. This is a curated list, not a sales chart: no units-sold figures, no trend data, and no popularity metrics are claimed. Every entry carries at least one verifiable source URL (teardown, manufacturer page, or reference article) and an evidence label. Entries that could not be sourced were excluded or replaced.
ranking_basis: Editorial ranking for hardware hackers. Not based on sales, shipments, revenue, search volume, or any measured popularity metric. Higher rank means the editors judge the device more relevant to teardown culture, chip curiosity, repairability, and hands-on hacking.

evidence_labels.confirmed: Multiple corroborating sources, including a published teardown.
evidence_labels.likely: At least one solid verifiable source (reference article or official product page).
evidence_labels.unconfirmed: Limited sourcing; official page unverified or thin corroboration.

selection_criteria: Device must have genuine hardware-hacker relevance (teardown interest, chip curiosity, repairability, or modding scene).
Device must have at least one verifiable public source URL.
No invented specifications, sales figures, or rankings.
Preference for devices with published teardowns or open hardware documentation.
Categories cover phones, SBCs, consoles, laptops, IoT, drones, VR, wearables, audio, tablets, networking, and hacker tools.

devices.why: A stamp-sized Linux computer on the MediaTek MT7688 with Wi-Fi and a microSD slot, useful for studying compact embedded Linux design and OpenWrt-derived firmware.

devices.name: Particle Argon
devices.why: Combines a Nordic nRF52840 with an ESP32 Wi-Fi coprocessor and an SWD debug connector on one Feather-format board, exposing dual-radio IoT architecture and cloud-managed firmware.

sources.note: Argon specifications: dual-radio design, SWD connector, Feather form factor
